title: The soup kitchen
hookLine: Ottoman imarets fed the poor daily

cards: A row of great copper pots, already bubbling before the sun is fully up. A cook stirs with a ladle as long as an arm.
Outside the door a line is forming: a student with a bowl, an old widow, a traveler still dusty from the road, a man who has not eaten since yesterday. Nobody asks for a coin, or a name.
The bowls go out full, and the cooks start the next pot. This isn't a story about one kind neighbor. It's about a building made to do this every day, whether anyone felt generous that morning or not.

teach.h: THE IMARET STOOD BESIDE THE MOSQUE.
teach.b: The Ottomans called it an imaret. Often it stood beside a mosque, inside a larger complex that might also hold a school, a guest house, sometimes a hospital.
The food came from the idea we met a few days ago, the waqf, the endowment.

teach.h: PAID FOR BY AN ENDOWMENT, FOREVER.
teach.b: Someone with means gave land or shops or rents forever, and the income paid for bread and soup, cooks and firewood, long after the giver was gone. So the meal at the door didn't depend on anyone's mood.

It was written into the deed. Who ate? The deeds that survive set out the order, and it varied from place to place: students and teachers, travelers, the poor of the neighborhood, the staff themselves.
Historians read them closely, because they show charity planned like a kitchen schedule. Why build such a thing?

The Qur'an describes the righteous this way, in Pickthall's words: "And feed with food the needy wretch, the orphan and the prisoner, for love of Him, (Saying): We feed you, for the sake of Allah only. We wish for no reward nor thanks from you."
No reward. Not even thanks. The bowl is not a trade.

teach.h: FEED THE HUNGRY: A PLAIN INSTRUCTION.
teach.b: And the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is reported in Sahih al-Bukhari to have told people to feed the hungry, visit the sick, and set captives free: one plain instruction in a short list.

teach.h: WE FEED YOU, FOR THE SAKE OF ALLAH ONLY.
teach.b: The imaret gave that line a roof, a chimney, and a budget, a promise kept in public. Soup for all.

how: Mosques and Muslim charities often run community kitchens and food drives, especially in Ramadan, when meals to break the fast are often shared freely with anyone who comes.

games.why: imarets were paid for by a waqf: land, shops or rents given forever, so the meal was written into the deed.

practice: Bring to mind one person who could use a meal: a neighbor who has been ill, a friend with a new baby, a coworker who skips lunch, or a stranger you'll never meet, through a food bank.
Picture the bowl or the bag of groceries reaching them, with nothing asked back. If you pray, hold that person in your prayer; if not, just keep their face in mind and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Imaret. The Ottoman kitchen beside the mosque, paid for by an endowment so the bowls went out every day. Today's word.
